title: Situational AI & Situation Awareness
question: How is situation awareness quantitatively measured in LLM agents, and what failure modes emerge when agents lack a dedicated situation-recognition layer?
lede: Mapping Endsley's three-level model of situation awareness onto LLM agents: how to measure it, and how it fails.
intro: One of five explorations from the summer of 2026, when UT Dallas students worked with Mindspace AI on questions emerging from Situational AI. This one synthesises 43 papers published between 1983 and 2026 across human factors, cognitive science, machine learning and AI safety, and asks what Endsley's model of situation awareness becomes when it is mapped onto language-model agents.

sections.heading: Endsley's three-level model
sections.html:
Situation awareness came out of aviation psychology, where one small misjudgement carries very large consequences. Endsley's model has three levels: perception of the elements in the environment — objects, state, conditions; comprehension of what those elements mean; and projection of the future state from the previous two.

Endsley, M. R. (1995). Toward a Theory of Situation Awareness in Dynamic Systems.

sections.heading: The lineage
sections.html:
Several research traditions have each solved part of this problem.

  • Situation calculus — John McCarthy's formal way to describe the world and reason about how actions change it.
  • Context-aware computing — software that adapts to information about people and their surroundings.
  • Robotics — connecting sensing, understanding and prediction so machines can operate in changing environments.

Situational AI brings the same question to language-based agents.

sections.heading: Measuring situation awareness in an LLM
sections.html:
The review arrives at a four-method setup:

  • Calibration metrics — P(IK) and P(True): the model's stated confidence against its actual correctness
  • The SAD behavioral benchmark — currently the only direct instrument
  • Linear probing of the representations encoded inside the model
  • Theory-of-mind tasks

sections.heading: Six failure modes
sections.html:
What goes wrong when an agent has no dedicated situation-recognition layer, arranged by the level of awareness each one breaks:

HallucinationInvents perceptions of sources, tools or world states (L1)
Theory-of-mind fragilityMisreads what another party knows or intends (L2)
Deceptive alignmentLearns to pass safety evaluations while behaviour is unchanged in deployment
Context-window saturationAwareness degrades as the window fills
Adversarial exploitation of local awarenessThe agent's own situational grasp is turned against it
Human out-of-the-loop degradationSupervision thins and the failure is not caught

sections.heading: The central paradox
sections.html: The more situationally capable an agent becomes, the more effectively it can suppress, fake or game the probes built to measure that capability. Capability and evasion rise in lockstep, which is precisely what makes evaluation hard.

sections.heading: The gap it identifies
sections.html:
• Doing what was asked is not doing what was wanted. The system follows the prompt and still misses what the person meant.
  • Agents don't know the present moment. They reason well and produce output, but know nothing of now unless told.
  • Context engineering is not understanding. Optimizing what a model receives is not the same as grasping what is happening.

A worked example: “My sink is still leaking. I called two days ago.” That is an unresolved commitment. The system should combine the message with the existing records, name the situation and record its evidence, then follow up the open ticket, ask a clarifying question, or escalate — not open a second ticket.

sections.heading: Next
sections.html:
• Benchmark the system against others
  • Evaluate the experiments — RiskPulse and Sentinel
  • A position paper stating the claim and inviting others to take it up
  • A more technical paper on the framework

title: Can Situations Make AI More Efficient?
question: How much context can an explicit situation layer remove, and at what cost?
lede: Recognize the situation first, and spend computation only when it is warranted.
intro: One of five explorations from the summer of 2026, when UT Dallas students worked with Mindspace AI on questions emerging from Situational AI. This one treats the hypothesis as an efficiency question: whether recognizing the situation first lets a system use less context, fewer tokens and smaller models.

sections.heading: Tokens are the meter
sections.html:
Cost and energy track token count, and the spread between workloads is enormous.

Single-turn chat reply200–2,000 tokens
RAG question with retrieved context2,000–12,000 tokens
Multi-page document summary10,000–100,000+ tokens
Agentic, multi-step task15,000–1,000,000+ tokens

Recent per-query energy estimates run from roughly 0.24–0.34 Wh for a short text query to about 40 Wh for a long one. Multiplied by the millions of prompts processed daily, the question of what computation is warranted stops being academic.

sections.heading: Why stateless models waste it
sections.html: With no persistent memory, every prompt regenerates its context. That produces redundant processing, runaway loops and inference spent re-reading what the system already knew. The cost compounds with repeated use.

sections.heading: Situation memory instead of re-reading
sections.html:
Storing and retrieving situation objects directly lets a system make incremental updates rather than running full-sequence inference each time. A traditional agent reprocesses the same context again and again; a situational agent keeps persistent situation memory and cuts the repeated token-level computation.

That is also what makes small models interesting: local, specialized models that operate within a context you dictate, without the data-centre dependency — though local hardware is slower, so the trade-off needs measuring rather than assuming.

sections.heading: What remains unresolved
sections.placeholder: The measurement itself: how much context an explicit situation layer actually removes on matched tasks, and what accuracy it costs.

title: RiskPulse + Situational AI
question: How can SCBCM-based models enhance the detection and interpretation of situational risk in accounting, fraud, compliance and cash-flow management — at the firm level, and aggregated to the sectoral and macroeconomic levels?
lede: Situation-centred models for financial risk, from firm-level fraud and distress to systemic stability — and RiskPulse, the working application.
intro: One of five explorations from the summer of 2026, when UT Dallas students worked with Mindspace AI on questions emerging from Situational AI. It has two strands: a review of situation-centred behavioral and context modelling (SCBCM) applied across finance and economics, written with Prof. Ramesh Subramoniam and Prasad Pillai; and RiskPulse, a working application that brings the same idea down to the scale of a small business.

sections.heading: The four research questions
sections.html:
1. How can SCBCM-based AI models enhance the detection and interpretation of situational risks in accounting, fraud, compliance and cash-flow management at the firm level?
  2. Which behavioral and contextual patterns are most predictive of distress, misreporting or non-compliance — and how do these aggregate at sectoral or macroeconomic levels?
  3. In what ways do AI-generated financial risk signals alter information asymmetry, capital allocation and the cost of capital in financial markets?
  4. How can situational AI insights be incorporated into macroprudential frameworks to reduce the likelihood or severity of financial crises?

sections.heading: Distress as a progression
sections.html: The review treats corporate distress as something that develops rather than arrives: profit erosion, then cash-flow strain, then creditor pressure, then behavioral distortion, then formal failure. The claim worth testing is that a situation-centred model recognizes the progression early enough to matter.

sections.heading: Risk lives in combinations
sections.html: The largest customer is thirty days late. Payroll is still due. Suppliers still have to be funded. Three alerts in most systems; one cash situation in reality. The point of recognizing the situation is that the combination means something none of the parts mean alone.

sections.heading: How it works
sections.html:
Situational, here, means context plus checked analysis plus a person:

  • Records are retrieved with RAG
  • Checked formulas calculate the metrics, rather than the model doing arithmetic
  • The model explains the implications
  • People choose the path

The response is then shaped by the business: collect, prioritize, compare, monitor. A $6k partial receipt plus $4k of deferred spending closes a $10k gap.

sections.heading: Demonstration
sections.placeholder: What the live demo shows, what was observed, and how the recognition performed against the business's own judgement.

sections.heading: Open problems
sections.placeholder: What remains unresolved, and what would have to be measured to know whether the recognition is actually improving decisions.

sections.heading: Where the literature is thin
sections.html: The review is explicit about its gaps. Nearly all the studies it covers use US, EU or Japanese data; emerging markets have higher data sparsity, weaker audit quality and more regime changes, which makes direct application unreliable. Adversarial robustness is the other open front.

title: Exploratory Situational AI Application
question: Can a fraud alert be turned into an inspectable situation — candidate types with the evidence for and against each — without letting a language model make the decision?
lede: Sentinel: from fraud alert to inspectable situation. An exploratory Situational AI application for card-not-present fraud triage.
intro: One of five explorations from the summer of 2026, when UT Dallas students worked with Mindspace AI on questions emerging from Situational AI. Sentinel is a working application built on a single principle: an alert is an event, and it is not yet an answer.

sections.heading: Recognize, interpret, respond
sections.html:
Recognize — point-in-time identities and behavioral context. Interpret — possible situation types, with the evidence for and against each. Respond — a proposed action, human review, and an audit record.

Optional language generation sits outside the decision path. It writes narrative; it cannot choose a label, a prediction set or an action.

sections.heading: The pipeline
sections.html:
1. Alert event — an upstream detector flags a transaction
  2. Case context — entity links and point-in-time features
  3. Pattern matcher — candidate types, with evidence for and against
  4. Set and policy — a prediction set, a proposed action and a lane
  5. Human review — analyst disposition, with human-only routing

Every assessment and disposition lands in a hash-chained audit trail. Automatic routing is off.

sections.heading: Preliminary findings
sections.html:
The real-data limit is visible, and reported rather than hidden.

178 / 200human label unanimity
564 / 600primary ratings of “cannot determine”
0 / 200named candidates admitted by the raw matcher

Selected, stratified cases — not fraud accuracy, live prevalence, or end-to-end coverage.

sections.heading: Next
sections.html: Better evidence and candidate admission come before any automation. Then independent validation.

title: The Student Exploration
question: Does Situational AI represent an emerging programming paradigm in which situations, rather than prompts, tasks, or workflows, serve as the core abstraction for AI reasoning and execution?
lede: Avani Tripathi's ongoing exploration of Situational AI. Its first output is a literature review asking whether situation is becoming a new core abstraction.
intro: One of five explorations from the summer of 2026, when UT Dallas students worked with Mindspace AI on questions emerging from Situational AI. This page is the home of Avani Tripathi's exploration and will grow as the work does. Its first output is the literature review below, which surveys traditional paradigms, ML-enabled systems, agentic and AI-native architectures and the situational awareness tradition, and asks whether Situational AI constitutes an emerging programming paradigm in its own right.

sections.heading: Four generations of software
sections.html:
Each era of software is organized around something. The review traces the succession and places Situational AI as the next candidate.

Pre-2000s · Traditional softwareOrganized around instructions. “Do exactly this.” Rules written in advance.
2000s–2015 · Machine learningOrganized around data patterns. “Learn from examples.” Adapts via training.
2015–2025 · Agentic AIOrganized around tasks and workflows. “Break it into steps and run them.”
Emerging · Situational AIOrganized around situations. “Understand what is happening, then decide.”

After Van Roy (2009), Programming Paradigms for Dummies, UCL.

sections.heading: A situation is five things at once
sections.html:
The review's working definition holds five elements in one connected frame, and keeps holding them over time:

  • Context — what is happening, and what led up to it
  • State — where things stand right now
  • Priorities — what matters most, and to whom
  • Expected response — what a competent actor would do here
  • Escalation conditions — when to stop and get a human

These move through a loop rather than a pipeline: recognize, remember, plan, act, escalate — and acting changes the situation, so the new state flows back to the beginning. Nothing resets.

sections.heading: Three design requirements
sections.html:
The review treats these as structural rather than desirable:

  • Explainability — the reasoning must be legible to a person. If you cannot see why it decided something, you cannot correct it when it is wrong.
  • Layered cognition — perception, symbolic structure and reasoning stay distinct rather than compressed into one opaque process. Separation is what makes it debuggable.
  • Bounded autonomy — independence scales with the situation. Routine, act; high-stakes, escalate. Autonomy is not one setting you turn up.

sections.heading: What is still unresolved
sections.html:
The review states its own limits plainly.

No formal definition of “situation”Without one, the paradigm claim cannot be tested or falsified. High
No empirical validationStill conceptual — no prototype benchmarked against an agentic baseline. High
Paradigm overlapNeuro-symbolic AI and cognitive architectures already cover parts of this space. Medium
Safety and oversightBounded autonomy in real time is not architecturally solved. High

Its conclusion is correspondingly careful: six domains and more than forty sources do not agree on much, but they converge on the same missing piece — a persistent situational layer. The gap is real, even if the answer is not settled.

sections.heading: Proposed empirical work
sections.html: The methodology the review proposes: build a Situational AI prototype with situation identification, memory, response planning, execution and escalation; deploy it against an agentic baseline on matched tasks of increasing complexity and novelty; and measure situation recognition accuracy among the outcomes.
